content: Oliver's sign refers to an abnormal downward movement of the trachea during systole, which can be indicative of a dilation or aneurysm of the aortic arch. To elicit Oliver's sign, the examiner gently grasps the cricoid cartilage and applies upward pressure while the patient stands with their chin extended upward. This phenomenon occurs due to the anatomical position of the aortic arch, which lies above the left main bronchus. If an aneurysm is present, a downward tug of the trachea may be felt during this maneuver. The sign was first described in 1878 by William Silver Oliver, an English military surgeon. Life-threatening causes of this sign include conditions that, if left untreated, may result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours.
